issues.issue: The legend states coverage is limited to claims "first made ... during the Policy Period or the Extended Reporting Period ... and reported in writing", but Section VI.A. (Awareness Provision) lets a noticed Potential Claim relate a later Claim back to an earlier period. A court could be asked to reconcile the absolute claims-made-and-reported condition with the relation-back mechanism.

The Retention is stated as applying to "Each Claim" without addressing how it applies when multiple Claims are deemed a single Claim under Section V.A. A dispute over the number of retentions is possible but the words are short and conventional.

The Declarations item is rendered "Item $6" while Sections II.C. and the body of the Policy repeatedly refer to "Item 5(A) in the Declarations" for the Extended Reporting Period premium. The mislabelled cross-reference could require construction of which item governs.

The check-box entry ("Yes J No[]") does not unambiguously record whether Punitive Damages Coverage was elected, and Section III.L. makes Punitive Damages coverage turn entirely on that election. Which box was marked is a construction question on the face of the document.

The entry "Yes E] No CE]" leaves it indeterminate on the face of the Declarations whether Third Party Claim Coverage was purchased, yet Insuring Agreement B and the Claim definition both operate "solely if Third Party Claim Coverage is included in Item 7". The election therefore has to be construed rather than read.

The Declarations record Terrorism Coverage as purchased with "No Separate Additional Premium", but no operative provision of the policy form grants, defines or limits any terrorism coverage. The scope of what was bought could only be determined from an endorsement not set out in the instrument.

The reporting condition combines an open-ended "as soon as practicable after any Insured first becomes aware of such Claim" with a fixed sixty-day outer limit, leaving it unclear whether notice inside sixty days but not "as soon as practicable" forfeits coverage. "Aware of such Claim" is itself undefined.

The grant covers a Wrongful Act "which takes place before or during the Policy Period", while Section V.A. and Section II.C. restrict coverage by reference to when Claims are deemed first made and Exclusion IV.A.2 cuts off pre-Pending-or-Prior-Date matters. Harmonising the temporal reach of the grant with those provisions is a live question.

The extension speaks of "all loss which such Spouse becomes legally obligated to pay" in lower case, while "Loss" is a defined and heavily limited term in Section III.L. Whether the undefined "loss" is broader than defined Loss is a genuine reading question.

The right arises only "if the Insurer chooses not to renew or the Parent Company cancels", which says nothing about an Insurer cancellation, although Section VIII.C.2 permits the Insurer to cancel for nonpayment. The omission raises an expressio unius question about when the Extended Reporting Period may be bought.

The clause both confines Extended Reporting Period cover to Claims "first made against the Insured during the Extended Reporting Period" and deems such Claims "to have been made during the immediately preceding Policy Period", a deeming that sits awkwardly with Section V.A.'s limit on "Claims first made during the Policy Period". Which characterisation governs could be argued.

"Any other such documents submitted in connection with the underwriting of this policy" is an open-ended catch-all appended to specific enumerated items, so the outer boundary of the incorporated Application is uncertain. The reach of that catch-all matters directly to the rescission/representation provisions.

"Any other payment to or for the benefit of an employee arising out of the employment relationship" is a general catch-all following specific items, cut back only by a carve-out for salary, wages and commissions. The boundary between excluded Benefits and covered damages is genuinely contestable.

"A written demand against any Insured for monetary or non-monetary relief" is the classic contested trigger: whether a letter, a charge, or a request for corrective action is such a demand is open. The reach of "similar formal proceeding before another federal, state or other governmental agency" is a further general-catch-all boundary.

Whether the term Claim includes Third Party Claims depends on the Item 7 election, which the Declarations record ambiguously ("Yes E] No CE]"). The operative definition therefore cannot be applied without construing Item 7.

"Reasonable and necessary legal fees and expenses" sets no benchmark, and the parenthetical carve-out for "other compensation of the Insured Individuals or Employees" against in-house defence work leaves a contestable boundary. Both are terms a fee dispute would turn on.

The definition covers only "Federal, State, or local" law yet extends "anywhere in the world", omitting foreign law that other provisions of the policy expressly name. That mismatch invites an expressio unius argument about foreign discrimination claims.

The final limb covers contractors "but only if such individual performs work or services solely for or on behalf of the Policyholder", and "solely" is undefined at the boundary of moonlighting or multi-client contractors. The list is also mis-numbered, with the fifth limb left unnumbered.

Independent contractors are Employees here, yet Section III.V. excludes Claims brought by independent contractors from Third Party Claims and Exclusion IV.A.9 excludes contract claims by contractors. The treatment of contractors across these provisions is hard to harmonise.

Limb 3, "illegal work related harassment", is an unbounded general term appended to two specific sexual-harassment limbs, raising an ejusdem generis question about non-sexual harassment. Its reach is not otherwise fixed by the policy.

Limbs 4 and 5 make cover for leased individuals and contractors depend on a written indemnity agreement "prior to any Claim", a condition whose satisfaction and scope ("matters within the scope of coverage of this Policy") is contestable. The term is otherwise conventional.

"Common nexus" of "any fact, circumstance, situation, event, transaction, cause or series of causally or logically connected" matters is notoriously indeterminate: "logically connected" has no stopping point. Because Section V.A. collapses interrelated acts into one Claim, the breadth of this phrase is directly outcome-determinative.

"The amount which the Insureds become legally obligated to pay on account of a Claim" is the standard battleground over whether restitutionary, equitable or statutory awards qualify. The inclusionary list is illustrative rather than exhaustive.

Sub-paragraphs 2 and 3 exclude "fines or penalties imposed by law" and "the multiple portion of any multiplied damage award", while Section III.L.'s punitive damages proviso and Section III.S. bring in liquidated damages under the ADEA, EPA and FMLA, which are penalty-like doubling awards. Those provisions cannot easily be read together.

"Matters uninsurable under the law applicable to this Policy" and "amounts for which the Insureds are legally or financially absolved from payment" are open-textured phrases with no fixed boundary. Their scope would have to be construed in any Loss dispute.

The clause directs that "the law of the jurisdiction most favorable to the insurability" governs among four listed connections, without saying who decides or how conflicting connections rank. "Most favorable" and the choice among (a)-(d) are open to argument.

This proviso restores Punitive Damages to Loss, but Section III.L.'s exclusions 2 and 3 (fines/penalties; the multiple portion of multiplied awards) would strip out the liquidated damages that Section III.S. defines as Punitive Damages. The two operate in opposite directions.

The list is mis-numbered (two items numbered 4, and a limb numbered 8 with no 6 or 7), and the closing proviso limits all of them to Claims "alleged as part of" other enumerated wrongs. Whether the proviso attaches to every limb or only the last is a real reading question.

The definition cross-refers to prior termination "in accordance with Section VLC", a section designation that does not exist; the cancellation provisions are in Section VIII.C. The broken cross-reference is a mechanical error in the provision.

The definition sweeps from EPA-listed hazardous substances to "noise", "odor" and "electromagnetic field", so the general expansion far outruns the enumerated hazardous-substance core. Whether the second and third sentences are limited by the first is arguable.

"An allegation or accusation ... provided such allegation does not constitute a Claim, but subsequently may give rise to a Claim" has no threshold: almost any complaint "may" give rise to a Claim. The boundary between a Potential Claim and a Claim is left to construction.

Defining Punitive Damages to include ADEA/EPA/FMLA liquidated damages collides with Section III.L.'s exclusion of "the multiple portion of any multiplied damage award" and of fines and penalties. The same award is both included and excluded depending on which provision is read first.

"The illegal retaliatory treatment of Employees, including any retaliatory treatment for" four listed activities leaves it open whether the list is exhaustive of protected activity. That matters because Exclusions IV.A.5 and IV.A.7 carve back for "any Claim for Retaliation".

The definition cross-refers to entities "covered pursuant to Section VHLA.1", a designation that does not exist in the policy (Section VIII.A.1 is presumably meant). The garbled cross-reference must be repaired before the definition can be applied.

"A customer or vendor of the Policyholder" (or a person "attempted to be" one) is undefined, and for a regulator like the named Parent Company it is far from obvious who counts as a customer. The carve-out for independent contractors sharpens rather than resolves the boundary.

Limb 3 extends to acts of "any other persons for whom the Insureds are legally responsible", an open-ended general category appended to two specific ones. Its reach beyond Insured Individuals is undefined.

Each limb is qualified only by the word "wrongful", which the policy nowhere defines, and limb 4 extends to any "adverse change in the terms, conditions or status of employment". The definition is circular at exactly the point a coverage dispute would arise.

The enumerated protected characteristics are followed by "or on any other basis prohibited by law", a catch-all whose relationship to the specific list is uncertain. Whether it is limited by ejusdem generis to comparable status-based discrimination is contestable.

Exclusion A.5 lists eight named statutes and then extends to "any other federal, state local or foreign statute or law similar to any statute or law described in (a) through (h)", so the reach of "similar" is a textbook general-versus-specific problem. Exclusion A.12's trigger phrase "if evidenced by ... a document or written statement by an Insured" is a second open boundary.

Exclusion A.8 excludes claims for "mental anguish, emotional distress, humiliation" but then carves back "any actual or alleged mental anguish or emotional distress in a Claim ... for a Wrongful Act by an Insured", which is the only kind of Claim the Insuring Agreements ever cover and which Section III.M. expressly makes an Other Workplace Tort. The exclusion and its carve-back cannot readily be reconciled.

Exclusion B.4 removes indemnity for "injunctive relief, declaratory relief, restitution, or any other equitable remedy", a catch-all whose scope against the enumerated examples is uncertain, especially as to restitution-like money awards. Exclusion B.1's carve-back for "any Claim for wrongful termination of employment" leaves a further boundary.

Exclusion B.4 strips indemnity for non-monetary relief although Section III.D. defines a Claim to include a written demand "for monetary or non-monetary relief" and Section III.L. defines Loss as amounts the Insureds are legally obligated to pay. Fitting these together on a mixed relief award is a genuine question.
